Michigan Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession FAQ

Can a squatter take ownership of my Michigan house?

Check the statute and talk to a Michigan attorney about your facts.

Can a squatter take ownership of a house in Michigan?

Only after holding the property openly, against the owner's rights, for the full statutory period, and then proving it in court. The period is 15 years in most cases. Moving into a vacant house does not create ownership in a month, a year or ten years.

Michigan has no separate squatter statute. The claim is adverse possession, which grows out of the limitation on actions to recover land in MCL 600.5801. When the time to sue for the land runs out, the owner loses the right to recover it.

Owners of vacant houses, inherited homes and rentals sitting empty between tenants are the ones most exposed, since a long stretch without anyone checking the place is what gives an occupant the continuous years the claim needs. Walking the property, keeping the taxes and utilities current in your own name, and giving written permission where a neighbor uses a strip all leave a record that helps later.

An owner who acts early never reaches that point. The tools for removing someone are quicker and cheaper in the first months than after years of acquiescence.

How long is the adverse possession period in Michigan?

The statute sets the time within which a person must sue to recover land or enter it. The length depends on how the person in possession claims title.

Time limits to recover land under MCL 600.5801
How the occupant claims titlePeriodSource
Deed from an executor, administrator, guardian or testamentary trustee, from a sheriff or other officer under court process, or from a sheriff on a mortgage foreclosure sale5 yearsMCL 600.5801(1)
Deed from an officer authorized to sell land for taxes10 yearsMCL 600.5801(2)
A devise in a will15 years after the will is probated in MichiganMCL 600.5801(3)
All other cases, including an occupant with no paper title15 yearsMCL 600.5801(4)

A person with no deed at all, who simply moves in, falls in the last row. That is why the 15-year figure is the one most owners ask about.

What must a claimant prove in a Michigan court?

The Court of Appeals repeats the same test in opinion after opinion. A claim requires clear and cogent proof that possession was actual, visible, open, notorious, exclusive, continuous and uninterrupted for the 15 years, and the burden of proof sits on the person who makes the claim.

  • Actual and visible: positive, affirmative acts of ownership, such as building, fencing, mowing or parking on the strip.
  • Open and notorious: so visible that the true owner is presumed to have notice, or the owner actually knew of the claim.
  • Hostile: use inconsistent with the owner's rights, without permission asked or given. It does not require ill will.
  • Exclusive and continuous: the claimant treated the land as their own to the exclusion of others for the full period, though constant use is not required and occasional trespasses by the owner do not defeat exclusivity.

Use with the owner's permission is not hostile, which is why a documented, revocable permission matters for a neighbor who has used part of a lot for years.

Can a claimant combine years with a previous owner?

Yes, if the claimant and the earlier occupant were in privity. Successive periods can be joined, or tacked, to reach 15 years. In an unpublished Court of Appeals opinion from June 2023, a business owner and two earlier owners of the parcel were found to be in privity, which let their years of using a drive, a parking lot and a septic field be added together.

Privity can be shown by including the disputed land in the deed, or by an actual transfer of possession of the disputed strip through statements made at the time of the conveyance. This is a common source of disputes after a sale, because a buyer may discover that the former owner's use of a strip has been counted toward a claim against the neighbor's lot.

What interrupts the clock?

Occasional entries do not. The same 2023 opinion explains that the period is interrupted only if the true owner reenters and stays in possession for at least one year, or files suit within one year of reentry. It cites MCL 600.5868 for that rule.

A quick fence-line walk or a chain across a driveway for a weekend leaves the clock running. An owner who suspects a claim should consult a Michigan attorney about a lawsuit instead of relying on informal gestures.

A related doctrine, acquiescence, can fix a boundary line without proof of hostility. A claim for the statutory period needs only that the neighbors treated a boundary line or marker as the property line for 15 years, and the standard of proof is a preponderance of the evidence.

How can an owner remove someone who has no right to be there?

Michigan allows summary proceedings to recover possession. Under MCL 600.5714(1)(f) a person entitled to possession can recover it from someone who took possession by forcible entry, holds by force after a peaceable entry, or came into possession by trespass without color of title or any other possessory interest.

Self-help is where owners get hurt. MCL 600.5711 bars entry unless the law permits it and, as a rule, requires a peaceable entry. Subsection (3) lets an owner enter without that limit when the occupant is a forcible-entry occupant or trespasser, but it states that a forcible entry does not include conduct covered by the assault chapter of the Michigan penal code.

Under MCL 600.2918, a person ejected by force is entitled to three times actual damages or $200, whichever is greater, plus possession, and a tenant can recover when an owner changes locks, removes doors, or cuts essential services. Subsection (5) says an owner does not unlawfully interfere with a trespasser who took possession by forcible entry or without color of title. If you are unsure whether the occupant is a tenant, treat them as one and use the eviction process.

What if the occupant was once a tenant or guest?

A former tenant or guest is not a trespasser. MCL 600.5714(1) gives separate routes for holding over after nonpayment of rent, for holding over after a lease ends, and for several other situations. For rent, the demand for possession gives the tenant 7 days to pay or leave.

If the owner's own title is clouded by someone else's long possession, the owner or the claimant can bring a quiet title action in circuit court under MCL 600.2932. Any person who claims a right in, or title to, land may sue anyone who claims an inconsistent interest, whether or not the defendant is in possession. The statute describes these actions as equitable in nature.

More questions about Michigan Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession

How many years until squatters have rights in Michigan?

Fifteen years in most cases under MCL 600.5801(4), and the claimant must still prove the elements by clear and cogent evidence. Shorter periods of 5 or 10 years apply when the occupant holds under certain court, sheriff or tax deeds.

Does paying the property taxes create ownership?

MCL 600.5801 says nothing about tax payment, and the elements recited by the courts do not include it. The elements are possession that is actual, visible, open, notorious, exclusive, hostile and continuous for the full period.

Can I change the locks on a squatter?

Only with care. A lockout can be unlawful if the person is a tenant, and MCL 600.2918 allows triple damages for a forcible ejection. Use summary proceedings under MCL 600.5714(1)(f) when the occupant entered by trespass.

Is permission a defense to a claim?

Yes, in the sense that hostile use is use without permission asked or given. Written permission makes it harder for a neighbor to show the hostility the claim requires.

What deadline applies to a lawsuit for lockout damages?

A claim to regain possession must start within 90 days after the cause of action arises or becomes known, and a damages claim within one year, under MCL 600.2918(8).

What the official sources say

  • For damage or other obligation against the deposit, the landlord must mail an itemized notice of damages within 30 days after termination of occupancy, with a check or money order for the difference (or electronic transfer within 10 days after mailing). (MCL 554.609(1)-(3); source)
  • The tenant must respond by mail within 7 days after receipt of the notice of damages or forfeits the amount claimed. (MCL 554.609(4); source)
  • An estate at will may be terminated by 1 month's notice; where rent is payable at periods under 3 months, notice equal to the rent interval is sufficient. (MCL 554.134(1); source)
  • Landlord covenants premises and common areas are fit for intended use and in reasonable repair, and complies with health and safety laws, unless disrepair caused by the tenant's wilful or irresponsible conduct; parties may modify only if the lease term is at least 1 year. (MCL 554.139(1)-(2); source)

Which Michigan landlord tenant rules matter when you sell a rental?

Four sets of rules touch a sale: the security deposit act, the covenants of fitness and repair, the notice rules that end a tenancy, and the summary proceedings that remove an occupant who will not leave. The deposit act is the one a seller cannot skip, because it keeps the old owner on the hook after the closing until the money is handled.

The Landlord-Tenant Act (1972 PA 348) says that when a landlord's interest ends by sale, assignment, death or otherwise, the landlord remains liable for the deposit until it is transferred to the successor with written notice to the tenant by ordinary mail, the successor posts the required bond, or the deposit is returned (MCL 554.614). A seller who closes without moving the deposit and notifying the tenant can still be sued for it.

  • Hand the deposit to the buyer, or return it, before or at closing.
  • Mail the tenant the buyer's name and address in writing.
  • Give the buyer the signed lease, the move-in checklist and the payment ledger.

How much security deposit can a Michigan landlord hold?

The ceiling is one and one-half months' rent (MCL 554.602). A landlord may demand a deposit only if the tenant is told in writing, within 14 days of taking possession, the landlord's name and address for notices, the name and address of the bank or surety holding the funds, and the duty to give a forwarding address within 4 days after moving out (MCL 554.603).

The money must sit in a regulated financial institution. A landlord may use it for other purposes only with a cash or surety bond filed with the secretary of state, covering deposits up to $50,000 and 25 percent of any excess (MCL 554.604). Until the landlord proves a right to it, the deposit is treated as the tenant's property (MCL 554.605).

Deductions are limited to actual damage beyond normal use, unpaid rent, rent due for early termination and unpaid utility bills (MCL 554.607). The landlord also has to use move-in and move-out inventory checklists (MCL 554.608). Buyers inheriting a tenant should ask for both, since a missing move-in checklist weakens any later damage claim.

What are the deadlines for returning a Michigan security deposit?

Within 30 days after the tenant moves out, the landlord must mail an itemized notice of damages with repair estimates, along with a check or money order for any balance. A September 2026 amendment now allows the balance to go by direct deposit or electronic transfer instead, within 10 days after the notice is mailed (MCL 554.609). If the landlord misses the 30 days, the law treats that as agreement that no damages are due, and the full deposit goes back right away (MCL 554.610).

The tenant answers by mail within 7 days. If the tenant never responds, or never gave a forwarding address, the landlord can generally keep the claimed amount. Where there is a real dispute, the landlord has 45 days after move-out to sue for a money judgment or return the balance. Failing to follow the section fully waives the damage claim and makes the landlord liable for double the deposit retained (MCL 554.613).

  • Day 4 after move-out: tenant's written forwarding address due.
  • Day 30: landlord's itemized notice of damages due.
  • Day 7 after receipt: tenant's mailed response due.
  • Day 45: last day for the landlord to file suit over a disputed amount.

What notice ends a Michigan tenancy?

It depends on the tenancy and the reason. An estate at will can be ended by either side with one month's notice, or a notice equal to the rent interval when rent is paid more often than every three months. A year-to-year tenancy ends one year after a notice to quit is served. A landlord can end any tenancy for unpaid rent with a written 7-day notice to quit (MCL 554.134).

A landlord can file for possession in a summary proceeding when a tenant holds over 7 days after a written demand for unpaid rent, and accelerated rent does not count as rent due for that purpose. Shorter periods apply to narrow cases: 24 hours for certain controlled-substance lease terminations after a police report, and 7 days after a notice to quit when a tenant or household member caused or threatened physical injury on the landlord's property (MCL 600.5714).

The same statute lets a person recover possession from someone who stays on after a mortgage or execution sale redemption period ends, or after a personal representative sells under court license or will authority. For an inherited rental, that matters: the buyer from an estate can use summary proceedings against a holdover.

What repair and lease-term rules follow the property to a new owner?

Every residential lease carries a covenant that the premises and common areas are fit for the use intended and kept in reasonable repair, with compliance with state and local health and safety laws. The exception is damage caused by the tenant's willful or irresponsible conduct. Parties can modify the covenant only when the lease term is at least one year (MCL 554.139). A buyer who plans to keep the tenant should walk the unit against that standard before pricing.

The Truth in Renting Act voids lease clauses that waive fitness remedies, waive deposit rights, allow confession of judgment, or let the lessor change terms mid-lease without written consent, with limited 30-day exceptions for tax and utility cost increases (MCL 554.633). If the lease you inherit contains such a clause, it will not hold up, and the buyer should not count on it.

Since April 2025, landlords with five or more rental units may not deny or end a tenancy because of a tenant's source of income, including vouchers and benefits. A tenant who proves a violation can recover actual damages or up to three times the monthly rent, whichever is less, plus costs and attorney fees (MCL 554.601c and 554.601d).

How long does it take to remove an occupant after a judgment?

For an ordinary eviction, the court cannot issue a writ of restitution until 10 days after the judgment for possession, with faster issuance in a few situations the court finds proven, such as forcible entry, trespass or a serious ongoing health hazard (MCL 600.5744). A tenant can stop the writ by paying the judgment amount and costs within the time allowed. If an appeal or new-trial motion is filed with a bond to stay proceedings, the waiting period is paused.

Officers carrying out a writ remove occupants and belongings and either leave the belongings in a public area or deliver them to the sheriff, so the removal itself is done by the court's officer.

ItemRuleSource
Deposit cap1.5 months' rentMCL 554.602
Notice of damagesMailed within 30 days of move-outMCL 554.609
Tenant responseMailed within 7 days of noticeMCL 554.612
Landlord suitWithin 45 days of move-outMCL 554.613
Nonpayment notice7 days, writtenMCL 554.134, 600.5714
Writ after judgment10 days in the ordinary caseMCL 600.5744

More questions about Michigan Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights

What happens to a tenant's security deposit when a Michigan landlord sells the house?

It must follow the property or go back to the tenant. The seller stays liable under MCL 554.614 until the deposit is transferred to the new owner with written notice to the tenant by ordinary mail, the new owner meets the bond requirement, or the deposit is returned.

How much notice does a Michigan landlord give to end a month-to-month tenancy?

One month, or a period equal to the rent interval if rent is paid at intervals shorter than three months. For nonpayment of rent the landlord may instead give a written 7-day notice to quit under MCL 554.134.

How long does a Michigan landlord have to return a deposit?

Thirty days after the tenant moves out to mail an itemized notice of damages and the balance. Missing that deadline means the full deposit must be returned, and an improper withholding can cost the landlord double the amount kept.

Can a Michigan landlord lock out a tenant after an unpaid rent notice?

No. Possession is recovered through summary proceedings, and a court officer carries out the writ of restitution. In the ordinary case the writ cannot issue until 10 days after the judgment for possession.

Do all Michigan landlords have to accept housing vouchers?

Landlords with five or more rental units in the state may not deny or end a tenancy based on source of income, including vouchers, since the 2025 amendment took effect. Owners of fewer than five units are outside that section.

Michigan Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Michigan Eviction Notice Rules sale

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Serious continuing health hazard or extensive physical damage: 7 days after demand to deliver up possession or substantially restore/repair. (MCL 600.5714(1)(d); source)
  • Controlled substance clause termination: 24-hour notice to quit (with formal police report); violence/threat of injury: 7-day notice to quit. (MCL 554.134(4); 600.5714(1)(b),(e); source)
  • Holdover after lease termination under a lease power, expiration of term, or notice to quit under MCL 554.134 supports summary proceedings; year-to-year tenancy terminated by notice to quit giving 1 year. (MCL 600.5714(1)(c); 554.134(3); source)
Selling in Michigan?
We buy Michigan houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What written notice must a Michigan landlord give before an eviction case?

Which notice applies turns on the landlord's reason. Unpaid rent brings a 7-day notice. A month-to-month tenancy ends on one month's notice, and a year-to-year tenancy ends one year after service. The legal source for most of these is MCL 554.134, with the court filing rules in MCL 600.5714.

Michigan's court administrators publish fill-in forms for each notice. The Demand for Possession for nonpayment is form DC 100a, the general Notice to Quit is DC 100c, and the drug activity notice is DC 100e. Every form comes in a tenant copy and a court copy; the landlord files away the court copy together with the record of how and when it was delivered.

What are the Michigan notice types and their time periods?

Michigan eviction notice types and days, from MCL 554.134 and MCL 600.5714
ReasonNotice periodStatute
Nonpayment of rent7 days554.134(2); 600.5714(1)(a)
Periodic or at-will tenancy1 month, or the rent interval when rent is paid more often than every 3 months554.134(1)
Year-to-year tenancyEnds 1 year after service554.134(3)
Controlled substance on the premises, with a formal police report24 hours554.134(4); 600.5714(1)(b)
Caused or threatened physical injury to someone, police notified7 days600.5714(1)(e)
Serious health hazard or extensive damage7 days after demand to leave or repair600.5714(1)(d)

What proof of service should a Michigan landlord keep?

The court's checklist for both the 7-day demand and the notice to quit has four steps, and a landlord who cannot answer yes to each may have trouble later in court:

  • Fill in the notice form completely, including the tenant's name, the delivery address, the rent owed or the move-out date, and the landlord's own address and phone.
  • Sign it.
  • Deliver the tenant's copy by one of the permitted methods.
  • Keep the court copy, whose certificate of service records the date of delivery, the name of the person who received it and how it was delivered.

That certificate becomes the landlord's evidence when the case reaches the judge, so it should be filled in on the day of delivery and not rebuilt afterward.

How must a Michigan landlord deliver the notice?

The court forms list four valid ways to serve it:

  • Hand it to the tenant in person.
  • Give it on the premises to a family or household member or the tenant's employee, with a request to pass it on.
  • Mail it first class to the last address you have for the tenant. For mail, MCL 600.5718 sets the service date as the next regular delivery day after mailing.
  • Email it, but only if the tenant has consented to electronic service in writing and the consent was confirmed by a reply.

The forms warn about improper service. Slipping the notice under the door, leaving it outside the door, attaching it to the property or mailing it by a method that requires a signature are all examples that can sink the later court case. The 7-day nonpayment form is the minimum, and the lease or another law may require a longer period.

What happens after the Michigan notice period ends?

The landlord can file a complaint in district court. The state court forms for the complaint ask for a copy of the notice or demand. The court then issues a summons.

  • Trial is set within 10 days of the summons being issued, and service must happen 3 or more days ahead of it. Courts with a local rule may instead require appearance 5 days after service.
  • A summary proceeding is heard within 7 days after the tenant appears or the trial date arrives, with adjournments only by stipulation.
  • A case based on the 24-hour drug activity notice is heard on the day the tenant appears and is adjourned only for extraordinary reasons.

If the court finds for the landlord on nonpayment, it fixes the amount due at trial and subtracts any rent excused by the landlord's breach of the lease or statutory covenants. The tenant can stop the writ by paying that amount plus taxed costs within the time provided (MCL 600.5741 and 600.5744(7)).

When can a sheriff or court officer actually remove a Michigan tenant?

Only after the court orders it. MCL 600.5744 directs the court to issue a writ of restitution commanding a court officer, bailiff or sheriff to put the landlord in possession and remove occupants and property. Ordinarily the writ waits for 10 days after judgment.

The court may allow an immediate writ on conditions it sets, for example when the premises have been ordered vacated for lack of a housing certificate, when entry was forcible, when the occupant is a trespasser, when the tenant is causing a serious health hazard or extensive damage, or in a drug activity case. A land contract forfeiture carries a longer wait: 90 days if under half of the price was paid, six months if half or more.

May a landlord change the locks or cut off utilities?

No. MCL 600.2918 treats force, changing locks without handing over keys, boarding up the premises, removing doors or windows, keeping or destroying the tenant's belongings, and cutting off heat, water, electric or gas as unlawful interference. The tenant may claim the larger of real damages or $200 for each incident.

Someone pushed out by force may recover triple actual damages or $200 if that is more, along with possession. A suit to regain possession is due within 90 days of the event or its discovery, and a damages suit within a year. The section cannot be waived in a lease. Exceptions cover court orders, brief entry for repairs or inspection, and good-faith belief that the tenant has abandoned and left rent unpaid.

What does a tenant mean for selling a Michigan house?

A rented house can often be sold occupied, yet a sale does not let the seller bypass the notice rules. The tenancy still ends only through the notice and court steps above, so a buyer who wants vacant possession has to wait out the lease or have the seller serve a proper notice first.

A few sale situations have their own rules. After a mortgage foreclosure sale or an execution sale, a person who stays in the house past the redemption period can be removed by summary proceedings under MCL 600.5714(1)(g). After a probate-licensed sale by a personal representative, the same remedy applies under paragraph (h). Following a foreclosure sale, the purchaser may inspect and, if inspection is unreasonably refused or damage is imminent, may start summary proceedings after giving the mortgagor 7 days' written notice to repair (MCL 600.3238).

Phone the clerk of the district court that covers the rental for local rules and the filing fee.

More questions about Michigan Eviction Notice Rules

How many days is a Michigan eviction notice for unpaid rent?

Seven days. A landlord may end the tenancy with a written 7-day notice to quit under MCL 554.134(2), and MCL 600.5714(1)(a) opens summary proceedings if the tenant stays past 7 days after a written demand. A lease may call for longer.

Can a Michigan landlord evict someone with a 24-hour notice?

Only for controlled substance activity when the lease has a termination clause and a formal police report has been filed. Under MCL 554.134(4) the notice is 24 hours. Other violations use longer notice periods.

Does a Michigan landlord need a court order to remove a tenant?

Yes. Yes. Once the notice runs out, the landlord files in district court, obtains a judgment and then waits for a writ of restitution, ordinarily 10 days later. Court officers or the sheriff carry it out.

What if a Michigan landlord changes the locks without a court order?

The tenant may recover actual damages or $200, whichever is greater, per occurrence under MCL 600.2918, and may recover possession. A tenant should file within 90 days to regain possession.

How much notice does a monthly tenant get?

One month. If rent is payable at intervals shorter than 3 months, the notice period equals the payment interval. A year-to-year tenancy ends 1 year after service of the notice.

What the official sources say

  • A $175 fee is added to each forfeited property. (MCL 211.78g(1); source)
  • Additional interest of 1/2% per month (noncompounded) on originally delinquent taxes, from the preceding March 1, applies on redemption. (MCL 211.78g(3)(b); source)
  • Absolute title and equity vest in the foreclosing governmental unit on the March 31 after judgment; persons with an interest may claim remaining proceeds after sale under section 78t. (MCL 211.78g(2); 2020 PA 256 note; source)

How does Michigan handle unpaid property taxes?

Michigan moves delinquent parcels through forfeiture to the county treasurer and then a court foreclosure. The statutes in the General Property Tax Act, MCL 211.78 and following, then provide for a sale or transfer of the foreclosed parcel under section 78m.

For an owner, the practical meaning is a fixed calendar. Taxes go delinquent, the parcel forfeits, a circuit court enters a foreclosure judgment, and redemption rights end on a set date after that judgment. Until that date the owner, or anyone with a legal interest in the property, can pay the redemption amount and stop the process.

That calendar is also the window in which a sale of the house can solve the problem, because a buyer's closing funds can pay the county treasurer before title passes to the government.

When does a Michigan property forfeit for unpaid tax?

On March 1 of each tax year, property that has been delinquent for taxes, interest, penalties and fees for the immediately preceding 12 months or more is forfeited to the county treasurer, along with certified abandoned property. That rule is in MCL 211.78g(1).

The treasurer adds a $175 fee to each forfeited parcel. Within 45 days after forfeiture the treasurer records a certificate with the register of deeds saying the property has been forfeited and not redeemed, and that absolute title will vest in the foreclosing governmental unit on the March 31 after a foreclosure judgment. The certificate must also explain a former owner's right to claim any remaining proceeds after a sale.

A county treasurer must withhold a property from forfeiture for any reason the State Tax Commission sets by rule.

How long does an owner have to redeem?

Redemption is open until the March 31 after the circuit court enters a judgment of foreclosure. In a contested case, it ends 21 days after the judgment. The judge must enter the judgment no later than March 30 following the hearing, according to MCL 211.78k(5).

To redeem, pay the county treasurer the full amount of unpaid delinquent taxes, interest, penalties and fees. Add interest at a noncompounded 1/2 percent per month, or fraction of a month, on the taxes originally returned as delinquent, counted from the March 1 before forfeiture, along with recording fees and the cost of serving notices. The treasurer may waive that extra interest when the property is withheld from the foreclosure petition under section 78h(3)(c).

What happens at the foreclosure hearing?

A person with an interest in a listed parcel may contest the forfeited taxes by filing written objections with the circuit court clerk and serving the foreclosing governmental unit before the hearing date. The grounds are narrow:

  • No law authorizes the tax.
  • The body that decides whether to levy a tax acted without jurisdiction or never imposed the tax.
  • The property was exempt, or the tax was not legally levied.
  • The tax was paid within the time allowed.
  • The tax was assessed fraudulently.
  • The property description was so vague or wrong that the forfeiture was void.

The court may also hold a property out of foreclosure for one year, or extend the redemption period, if the owner is a minor heir, is incompetent, is without means of support, or faces substantial financial hardship. A taxing unit's lien is not harmed by that delay, and the parcel returns to the next year's proceeding.

What does the foreclosure judgment do to the title?

If nothing is paid by the redemption deadline, fee simple title vests absolutely in the foreclosing governmental unit. The judgment extinguishes all liens against the property, including tax and special assessment liens, apart from future special assessment installments and certain state environmental liens. It also ends every recorded and unrecorded interest, with exceptions for visible or recorded easements, private deed restrictions, certain oil and gas interests and a few others.

After that date the judgment generally cannot be modified, stayed or held invalid. Appeals go to the Court of Appeals on the circuit court record, and a person appealing must pay the county treasurer the amount found due by the deadline, with the notice of appeal. If the foreclosure is affirmed, the money is refunded.

If a property is redeemed, the treasurer issues a redemption certificate, and one copy is recorded with the register of deeds. Unpaid taxes that were never returned as delinquent are not extinguished by that redemption.

Are there payment plans or reductions for owner-occupants?

Yes, for a principal residence that is exempt from the school operating tax. Under MCL 211.78q, a foreclosing governmental unit may offer a delinquent property tax installment plan to a financially distressed owner, and a county treasurer may sign a tax foreclosure avoidance agreement of up to 5 years for residential property once the owner makes an initial payment the treasurer sets.

  • While an agreement is in effect, the property is withheld from the foreclosure petition and interest runs at 1/2 percent per month, noncompounded, counted from the date the taxes were originally returned as delinquent, in place of the extra interest counted from March 1.
  • A treasurer may not sign more than 2 agreements with the same owner.
  • If the owner defaults, the extra interest applies and the parcel goes into the next foreclosure petition.

Participating local units may also adopt a payment reduction program described in MCL 211.78g(8). Ask the county treasurer which of these programs the county offers, since each county decides what it makes available.

Can a former owner claim money after a tax foreclosure sale?

Yes. Michigan law lets a person who held a legal interest just before the foreclosure judgment took effect claim the remaining proceeds from a later sale. The amount is what the sale brought in, minus the minimum bid, the other costs of the forfeiture, foreclosure, sale and upkeep, and a 5 percent sale commission, under MCL 211.78t.

The process runs in two steps:

  • By July 1 after the foreclosure takes effect, send the foreclosing governmental unit a notarized notice on the Treasury form, by personal service or certified mail.
  • After receiving the unit's notice, file a motion with the circuit court during the window from February 1 to May 15 following the sale or transfer.

The claimant carries the burden of proof, and the right cannot be transferred except by will or intestate succession. Both dates come from the statute, so calendar them as soon as the foreclosure is effective.

Why sell before the foreclosure judgment?

Once the judgment is effective, the owner loses the house and every equity dollar in it, except what a successful remaining-proceeds claim returns after the government sells. A sale before the redemption deadline can pay the treasurer's payoff figure at closing and leave the seller with the difference.

Ask the county treasurer for a written payoff that includes interest, fees and recording costs, and for a redemption certificate once the money is paid. Confirm with the register of deeds that the certificate is recorded. If the redemption deadline is close, tell the title company at the start so that wire and recording steps fit before it.

More questions about Michigan Tax Deed and Tax Lien Sales

Does Michigan sell tax lien certificates to investors?

The unpaid-tax statutes provide for forfeiture to the county treasurer and a court foreclosure, followed by a sale or transfer under MCL 211.78m. Ask the county treasurer how the county handles foreclosed parcels.

When is my redemption deadline?

It is the March 31 after the judgment of foreclosure, or 21 days after the judgment in a contested case. The county treasurer can confirm the date for your parcel.

What is the extra fee on a forfeited property?

The county treasurer adds $175 to each forfeited property. Redemption also adds 1/2 percent per month, noncompounded, on the originally delinquent taxes from the March 1 before forfeiture.

Can I still claim money if the county sells my foreclosed house?

You may. A person with a legal interest just before the judgment can claim remaining proceeds, starting with a notice due by July 1 after the foreclosure takes effect and a court motion filed between February 1 and May 15.

Can the court delay a foreclosure for hardship?

Yes. For a minor heir, an incompetent owner, an owner without means of support or one in substantial financial hardship, the court may hold the property out for one year or extend the redemption period.
